method: Paper 1: title, citation, DOI, design and abstract read on its PubMed record (PMID 9880251). Paper 2: PubMed returned a captcha page, so title, authors, citation, DOI, PMID and abstract were read on the Arizona State University research record of the Science paper.

claims.claim: When 16 non-obese adults were overfed by 1000 kcal a day for 8 weeks, fat storage differed about tenfold between people, and those whose non-exercise activity (NEAT: posture, fidgeting, daily movement) rose more gained less fat.
claims.source_title: Role of nonexercise activity thermogenesis in resistance to fat gain in humans
claims.authors: Levine JA, Eberhardt NL, Jensen MD
claims.study_type: Controlled overfeeding trial, 16 non-obese volunteers, +1000 kcal/day for 8 weeks
claims.finding: Abstract: two-thirds of the rise in daily energy expenditure came from NEAT; NEAT changes accounted for the 10-fold differences in fat storage; change in NEAT predicted resistance to fat gain (r = 0.77, P < 0.001).

claims.claim: Mildly obese sedentary adults sat about 2 hours a day longer than lean ones.
claims.source_title: Interindividual variation in posture allocation: possible role in human obesity
claims.authors: Levine JA, Lanningham-Foster LM, McCrady SK, Krizan AC, Olson LR, Kane PH, Jensen MD, Clark MM
claims.study_type: Observational study, 10 lean and 10 mildly obese sedentary volunteers, posture and movement recorded every half second for 10 days
claims.finding: Abstract: obese individuals were seated, on average, 2 hours longer per day than lean individuals; posture allocation did not change with weight loss or gain; adopting lean people's NEAT could expend an estimated additional 350 kcal per day.

limitations: Both studies are small (16 and 20 people) and the 2005 study is observational, so it shows an association, not that sitting causes obesity. The 350 kcal figure is a model estimate and is left out of the script. The script says 'small study', and hedges the takeaway with 'قد'.
